description: The people came to Jeremiah in crisis and promised to obey whatever God said. He made them wait ten days before He answered.
excerpt: Ten days can feel like an eternity in a hard situation. When you're scared, when decisions need to be made, waiting even a few hours for clarity feels impossible.
verse: "Ten days later the Lord gave his reply to Jeremiah."
body_html:
Ten days.

I highlighted this verse because of that specific number. The people had come to Jeremiah in crisis. They needed to know whether to stay in Judah or flee to Egypt. They promised they'd obey whatever God said. And God made them wait ten days for the answer.

Ten days can feel like an eternity in a hard situation.

When you're scared, when decisions need to be made, waiting even a few hours for clarity feels impossible. Ten days? Most of us wouldn't make it that long. We'd assume God isn't going to answer, decide He must want us to just make our best guess, and move ahead. We'd tell ourselves He'd redirect us if we were wrong, and quietly stop asking.

But God did answer. It just took time.

The harder thing is that this is a balance I still haven't figured out. There have been seasons in my life where I genuinely didn't know what God was saying. I prayed. I asked. I read His Word. And still, no clear answer. At what point do you move? At what point do you keep waiting?

I don't think there's a formula. But a few things have helped me over the years.

Sometimes the waiting itself is the answer. God isn't slow, and He's not distracted. If He's silent, there's a reason. He may be growing something in me during the wait, or protecting me from a decision I'd make too quickly, or letting other pieces move that I can't see yet.

Other times, movement is what clarifies things. Taking one small step in a direction and paying attention to whether God confirms or blocks it is different than making the whole decision without Him.

And sometimes waiting is obedience. The people in Jeremiah's story eventually got their answer, but they'd already decided what they wanted to do. When God said stay in Judah, they went to Egypt anyway. Their impatience wasn't just impatience. It was the beginning of disobedience.

I don't want to be that. I want to be someone who waits when God asks me to wait, moves when He asks me to move, and keeps asking until I actually hear from Him, and not just what I want to hear.

Even if it takes ten days. Or longer.

Are you in a season of waiting on God right now, and are you asking Him for direction or just filling the silence with your own plan?
